name: Fine-Grained and Thematic Evaluation of LLMs in Social Deduction Game (Microscopic Analysis on LLM Players via Social Deduction Game)
authors_org: Byungjun Kim, Dayeon Seo, Minju Kim, Bugeun Kim (Chung-Ang University; ELU Lab) [uncertain]
games_supported: Spyfall (a social deduction game where one or more 'spies' do not know a shared secret location and must blend in via question-and-answer rounds)
hidden_role_mechanic: Asymmetric information via a hidden spy role: non-spy players share a common location/topic while the spy is uninformed and must infer it; spies attempt to evade detection while non-spies attempt to expose the spy through indirect questioning
rule_variant_coverage: Single game (Spyfall); the work focuses on one ruleset rather than multiple role-set variants, and acknowledges limited generalization across game types [uncertain]
multimodal_support: No; purely text-based evaluation with no video, audio, or voice-prosody modalities
reasoning_paradigm: Prompted LLM agents performing question-asking, answering, accusation and deduction in natural language; no specialized search or RL policy is used (the contribution is evaluation methodology, not a new reasoning architecture)
memory_mechanism: Game dialogue history is supplied to the LLM as conversational context within the prompt; no external memory store or learned memory module is introduced [uncertain]
belief_state_representation: Beliefs about who is the spy are expressed implicitly in natural-language reasoning and accusation outputs rather than as an explicit probability table or latent state [uncertain]
planning_approach: No explicit planning, tree search, or latent-space planning; agents act turn-by-turn from prompted reasoning [uncertain]
action_tool_design: Game actions (asking a question, answering, accusing a suspected spy) are elicited as structured natural-language outputs from the LLM within a scripted Spyfall game loop rather than as formal tool/function calls [uncertain]
theory_of_mind_evaluation: ToM is assessed indirectly: the fine-grained metrics for inferring subtext, evading suspicion, and information gathering probe whether models reason about other players' knowledge and intent, but there is no dedicated belief-accuracy ToM benchmark [uncertain]
turn_structure: Sequential rounds in which players take turns asking and answering questions; an accusation/voting step follows the question-answer rounds [uncertain]
phase_handling: Distinct phases for question-and-answer exchange and for accusation/decision are managed by a scripted Spyfall game controller [uncertain]
communication_protocol: Public natural-language question-and-answer exchanges among all players, followed by a public accusation; no private channels
communication_synchrony: Synchronous, turn-based: players speak in a fixed sequential order managed by the game controller [uncertain]
metrics: Six fine-grained metrics replacing outcome-only win-rate measurement, plus a structured thematic analysis. The six metrics cover accusation/deduction accuracy, defense and suspicion-evasion, information gathering, role comprehension, strategic consistency, and overall deduction quality (event-level behavioral measures) [uncertain]
deception_metric_design: Deception is captured through suspicion-evasion and defense metrics measuring how well the spy avoids being accused, rather than via an explicit lie taxonomy or detector-accuracy surrogate [uncertain]
persuasion_modeling: Persuasive influence is not explicitly modeled or optimized; the focus is on diagnostic fine-grained skill evaluation
rating_system: No competitive rating system (no Elo/TrueSkill/Swiss); models are compared on the six fine-grained metric scores with statistical significance testing (Kruskal-Wallis) [uncertain]
competition_format: LLM-vs-LLM self-play game sessions used as a measurement harness; no cross-play tournament
human_baseline_comparison: Limited or no direct head-to-head human-vs-LLM play; the study centers on model-to-model comparison and thematic error analysis rather than a human baseline [uncertain]
data_source_provenance: Synthetic LLM-vs-LLM gameplay generated by running the Spyfall environment, analyzed with quantitative metrics and qualitative thematic coding
training_paradigm: Tuning-free prompting; no SFT, RL, or DPO is applied. The contribution is an evaluation framework, not a trained agent
agent_controllability: Not applicable; agent skill is not tuned to a target win rate or difficulty
strategy_space_analysis: Emergent failure modes are analyzed thematically (four reasoning-failure categories) rather than emergent winning strategies or strategy-space expansion
prompt_optimizer_used: None; no DSPy or prompt-optimization method (GEPA, MIPROv2, BootstrapFewShot, SIMBA) is used
rl_algorithm: None; no RL or preference-optimization algorithm is used
reward_design: Not applicable; no training signal or reward is defined since agents are not trained
optimization_target: Not applicable; nothing is optimized (evaluation-only study)
self_play_loop: LLM-vs-LLM self-play is used only to generate gameplay data for evaluation, not for iterative training
credit_assignment: Not applicable; no credit assignment since no learning occurs. The methodological contribution instead replaces coarse outcome credit with event-level fine-grained metrics
optimization_cost: Not applicable; no training compute (inference-only evaluation runs) [uncertain]
framework_used: Custom Spyfall game environment (elu-lab/spygame) driving prompted LLM agents; no DSPy or LangChain [uncertain]
open_source: Yes; code is released at github.com/elu-lab/spygame
reproducibility: Moderate; the game environment and code are public, though full configs, seeds, and dataset release completeness are not fully confirmed [uncertain]
key_results: The paper argues that coarse outcome-only metrics and unstructured error analysis are insufficient for evaluating LLM social-deduction players. It introduces six fine-grained, event-level metrics and a thematic analysis yielding four major reasoning-failure categories (reward hacking, hallucination, bias, and dissociation between stated understanding and actual decisions). LLMs were found to perform notably better at logical deduction than at role-playing tasks such as inferring subtext and evading suspicion, with statistically significant performance variance across GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and Llama 2 (GPT-4 strongest overall) [uncertain]
identified_limitations: Findings may not generalize across diverse game types and player counts since only Spyfall is studied; the evaluation depends on a single ruleset and limited model set [uncertain]
deception_emergence: Models show measurable but uneven deceptive/evasive ability: they struggle to evade suspicion and to infer subtext, and exhibit failure modes such as hallucinating game state and dissociation between stated understanding and chosen actions, indicating fragile rather than robust deception [uncertain]
deceiver_detector_asymmetry: The fine-grained results suggest LLMs are relatively weak at the role-playing/concealment (deceiver) side compared with logical deduction (detector) side, implying they are stronger as deduction reasoners than as evasive deceivers [uncertain]
